newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ yield curve ends steeper on short-end strength.
newsitem.headline: NZ yield curve ends steeper on short-end strength.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 92.92 (PREV 92.87) 90-DAYS 7.12 (PREV 7.15)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.10 PCT (PREV 7.05) US 5-YR 6.58 (PREV 6.58)
MCI -74 VS -70
* NZ yield curve steepens at close, flows light
* Long bonds lag, end two pips weaker
* Potential seen for buying ahead of Tuesday's PPI
New Zealand's yield curve steepened at Monday's close as the slightly stronger short end was followed by a more reluctant long bond.
The 90-day bank bill rates closed down three basis points at 7.12 percent against their 7.17 percent open, while the mid bonds strengthened by three b.p. to end at 7.27 percent.
Meanwhile at the long end the 11/06 maturity yield finished two b.p. higher at 7.57 percent, after opening up four.
Dealers said bidding interest had surfaced in the short end in the afternoon, but with the U.S. and U.K. markets out for public holidays volumes had been fairly light.

April's merchandise trade surplus of NZ$55 million was worse than the market had expected (+$80 million), but dealers said the data had no implications either for rates or the currency. March quarter Producers Price Index data due on Tuesday at 2245 GMT might provide more insight into the state of the economy, they said.
"We need some more information to come out. There is nothing really to trade on -- the market is pretty fairly priced at the moment," one commented.
Market commentators MMS Pacific suggested the 90-days' close below 7.16 percent would lend the short end a firm technical tone for moves toward 7.04 percent.
"Driving these lower yields will either be a sharply higher USD (NZD seems stuck to tight ranges for now), or buying interest ahead of PPI data tomorrow," MMS Pacific said.

A Reuters poll of economists gave an average expectation of a 0.5 percent rise in the inputs index for the March quarter (up 0.15 percent annually), and a 0.1 percent rise in the outputs index (up 0.15 percent annually).
-- Catherine McCaw, Wellington newsroom (64 4) 471 4275
